content: What can we do with a big unlabelled chunk of DNA (e.g., parts of a newly sequenced genome) ?

label: text

label: text
content: ## → How do we model DNA sequences?

label: text
content: An alignment profile/motif is a model for a specific DNA pattern (e.g., a binding site)!

label: text
content: Once defined the model, we can employ it to find other instances of the pattern in new sequences

label: text
content: Do some regions in the new sequences "fit the model" well?

label: text
content: - Compute overall probabilities for regions based on the frequencies (=probabilities) of individual symbols in the motif!

label: text
content: Drawback of modeling sequences by means of profiles/motifs:

label: text
content: - Like in the motif, all other instances of the pattern are assumed to have the same length w

label: text
content: This works well only for certain cases, e.g., transcription factor binding sites

label: text
content: How can we build a sequence model for more general cases, i.e., to model and find interesting genomic regions of variable length?

label: text
content: - Examples of functionally relevant regions of variable length:

label: text
content: ★ CpG islands (contain a high frequency of C followed by G)

label: text
content: - Protein-coding genes (different numbers of exons and variable exon length!)

label: text
content: Example: difficulty of modeling and finding protein-coding genes

label: text
content: - The coding region starts with "ATG", has a length that is a multiple of 3 (codons), and ends with a stop codon—either "TGA", "TAA" or "TAG"

label: text
content: The total length can be very different

label: text
content: - The coding regions are usually interrupted by intronic regions which are spliced out!

label: text
content: - Since genes can encode for very different proteins, we can expect no sequence similarity at all (apart from the start and stop codons)

label: text
content: Can we still build a model for this and use it to identify new genes in the genome?

label: text
content: - Ability to emit (or generate) DNA sequences of a certain type (e.g., simulate promoters)

label: text
content: Not exact alignment to previously known gene, promoter, etc.

label: text
content: Preserving 'properties' of type, not identical sequence

label: text
content: ## Markov Chains and Hidden Markov Models

label: text
content: - Probability provides a calculus for manipulating models

label: text
content: - Not limited to yes/no answers - can provide "degrees of belief"

label: text
content: - Many common computational tools are based on probabilistic models

label: text
content: - Our tools: Markov Chains and Hidden Markov Models (HMMs)!

label: text
content: - Russian mathematician, known for his work on stochastic processes

label: text
content: "Markov" chains were the primary subject of his research

label: text
content: ## Markov Chains and Hidden Markov Models

label: text
content: - A sequence of data items (e.g., sequence of symbols/letters) is generated by a model (can be described by a graph) which has:

label: text
content: ★ certain transition probabilities (weighted edges) between the states

label: text
content: - The model transitions between different states like in a Markov Chains

label: text
content: - But: the states are not directly observable ("hidden")!

label: text
content: - Instead: each state has associated emission probabilities to generate certain observable data items (symbols)

label: text
content: - That is: the observed sequence of data items was generated by the model transition through different states which are, however, not directly observable

label: text
content: ★ The set of hidden states is usually not identical/equivalent to the set of emitted symbols/letters!

label: text
content: - In other words: we don't know in which state the model is in, we only observe which characters the model is emitting!

label: text
content: - What you see is what you get (states are directly observed)

label: text
content: - Next state only depends on current state (no memory!)

label: text
content: - Hidden state (e.g., season, storm system) determines probabilities of observations (e.g., weather)

label: text
content: - State transitions are governed by a Markov chain

label: text
content: - Transition probability from hidden state k to hidden state I

label: text
content: - Emission probability of symbol $x_{i}$ when the hidden state is $k$

label: text
content: - Vector $\pi = (\pi_{1},\pi_{2},\dots)$ : hidden path (sequence of hidden states of a set $\Sigma$ )

label: text
content: - Vector $x = (x_{1}, x_{2}, \dots)$: sequence of observations of a set $V$ of $m$ symbols

label: text
content: - Transition matrix $A= \left( a_{k l} \right)$ : probability of $k \to I$ state transitions

label: text
content: - Emission vector $E_{k} = \left(e_{k}\left(v_{1}\right),\dots,e_{k}\left(v_{m}\right)\right)$: prob. of observing the possible observable letters $v_{j}\in V$ from state $k$

label: text
content: - Emission matrix: contains emission probabilities for all states

label: text
content: - Bayes' rule: use $P \left( x_{i} \mid \pi_{i}=k \right)$ to estimate $P \left( \pi_{i}=k \mid x_{i} \right)$

label: text
content: Definition: A Markov chain is a triplet $(Q,p,A)$, where:

label: text
content: - $Q$ is a finite set of states; each state corresponds to a symbol in the alphabet $\Sigma$

label: text
content: - p is a vector of initial state probabilities

label: text
content:
- $A$ is the matrix of state transition probabilities, denoted by $a_{kl}$ for each $k, l \in Q$

- For each $k, l \in Q$ the transition probability is: $a_{kl} \equiv P(x_i = l | x_{i-1} = k)$

label: text
content: Output: The output of the model is the state at each instant time (path) $\rightarrow$ the states are directly observable

label: text
content: Property: The probability of each observed symbol $x_{i}$ (= state $q\in Q$ at time step i) depends only on the value of the preceding symbol $x_{i-1}$ :

label: text
content: - In other words: transition probabilities to the next state depend only on the current state, not on the previous path that led to it (no memory)!

label: text
content: Formula: The probability of observing a specific sequence $x$ of length $L$ is:

label: formula
content:
$$
P (x) = P \left(x _ {L}, x _ {L - 1}, \dots , x _ {1}\right) = P \left(x _ {L} \mid x _ {L - 1}\right) \times P \left(x _ {L - 1} \mid x _ {L - 2}\right) \times \dots \times P \left(x _ {2} \mid x _ {1}\right) \times P \left(x _ {1}\right)
$$

label: text
content: where $P \left( x_{1} \right)$ is the initial state probability of $x_{1}$

label: text
content: ## Components of a Hidden Markov Model (HMM)

label: text
content: Definition: An HMM is a 5-tuple (Q,V,p,A,E), where:

label: text
content: - $Q$ is a finite set of states $q_{n}$; $|Q| = N$

label: text
content: - $V$ is a finite set of observable symbols $v_{m}; |V| = M$

label: text
content: - p is a vector of initial state probabilities

label: text
content:
- $A$ is the matrix of state transition probabilities, denoted by $a_{kl}$ for each $k, I \in Q$

- For each $k, I \in Q$ the transition probability is: $a_{kl} \equiv P(x_i = I|x_{i-1} = k)$

label: text
content:
- $E$ is an $N\times M$ emission probability matrix,

$e_{nm}\equiv P(x_{i}=v_{m}\in V$ at step $i|\pi_{i}=q_{n}\in Q)$

label: text
content: Note: $e_{nm}$ does not depend on the time step i, i.e., emission probabilities of the symbols $v_{m}\in V$ depend only on the states $q_{n}\in Q$ and don't change over time!

label: text
content: Output: Only emitted symbols from V are observable by the system but not the underlying random walk between states from $Q \rightarrow$ "hidden"!

label: text
content: Property: Both emissions and transitions are dependent on the current state only and not on the past (no memory)!

label: text
content: A typical representation of a process which can be modeled by an HMM:

label: text
content: - Start: a random initial state $\pi_{1} \in Q$ according to the initial state probabilities $p$

label: text
content: Note: in this depiction, state $\pi_{0}$ represents a sort of "null" state before the process starts; the transition from $\pi_{0}$ or $\pi_{1}$ represents the choice of the first/initial state $(\pi_{1})$

label: text
content: - The random choice to move from the current (hidden) state $\pi_{i-1}=k\in Q$ to the next (hidden) state $\pi_{i}=I\in Q$ depends on transition probabilities $a_{kl}$

label: text
content: - The set of possible random choices also includes $k \rightarrow k$; so if $a_{kk} \neq 0$, it is possible that $\pi_i = \pi_{i-1}$, i.e., the system remains in the same state

label: text
content: - For each step $i$ of the hidden path, the hidden state $\pi_{i}$ randomly emits an observable symbol $x_{i} \in V$ according to the emission probabilities $e_{\pi_{i}} \left( x_{i} \right)$

label: text
content: For example, let the current hidden state be "summer"; this defines the probabilities of observing different weather: "sun", "clouds", "rain", "snow", ...

label: text
content: For the hidden state "winter", instead, the same weather "symbols" can be observed, but with significantly different "emission" probabilities!

content: # Prediction of Complete Gene Structures in Human Genomic DNA

label: text
content: We introduce a general probabilistic model of the gene structure of human genomic sequences which incorporates descriptions of the basic transcriptional, translational and splicing signals, as well as length distributions and compositional features of exons, introns and intergenic regions. Distinct sets of model parameters are derived to account for the many substantial differences in gene density and structure observed in distinct C + G compositional regions of the human genome. In addition, new models of the donor and acceptor splice signals are described which capture potentially important dependencies between signal positions. The model is applied to the problem of gene identification in a computer program, GENSCAN, which identifies complete exon/intron structures of genes in genomic DNA.
